title: Transformers and attention, in plain terms

sources.claim: Vaswani et al. (2017), "Attention Is All You Need", introduced the Transformer, a network built on attention without recurrence, first posted in June 2017; transformers became the basis of most later large language models.

sections.skill: Explain attention in transformers at a conceptual level

questions.prompt: What is the key idea of the transformer design?

choices.text: Following grammar rules typed in by linguists
Attention: weighing how relevant other words are
Memorizing every sentence ever written word for word
Reading only one word at a time with no context

questions.correct_answer: Attention: weighing how relevant other words are
questions.intro: Most modern language models use a design called the TRANSFORMER, introduced in a 2017 research paper. Its key idea is ATTENTION: when the model processes one word (token), it can weigh how relevant every other word in the context is. In "The trophy did not fit in the suitcase because it was too big," attention helps link "it" with "trophy." The model computes these weights with math, many times over, in many layers, which lets it track relationships across long passages. Attention is a mathematical weighting of text, not a mind paying attention the way a person does.
questions.feedback: Attention links words to relevant context.

questions.prompt: In the example, which word gets the heaviest highlight for "she"?
questions.correct_answer: Maria
questions.intro: When you read "Maria gave Sam her umbrella because she was leaving early," you might mentally connect "she" to "Maria." Imagine marking how strongly each other word helps you understand "she": a heavy highlight on "Maria," a lighter one on "leaving," almost none on "umbrella." A transformer does something like this with numbers for every word: it computes weights showing how much each other word should influence the current one. The highlights are a teaching picture; the real thing is arithmetic done many times.

sections.title: Apply it

questions.prompt: A model links "it" to the wrong noun in a tricky sentence. What does this show?

choices.text: The model was not using attention at all
Attention can weigh the wrong words

questions.correct_answer: Attention can weigh the wrong words
questions.intro: The word "attention" invites human comparisons, so be careful. A model's attention weights are numbers computed from patterns; they are not feelings, intentions or awareness. Attention also does not guarantee correct understanding: a model can weigh the wrong words and link "it" to the wrong noun, especially in tricky sentences. Researchers sometimes inspect attention weights to study models, but high attention on a word does not by itself prove the model "understood" that word or used it for the reason a person would.
